procedural_history.originating_court: Inferred to be a lower court/tribunal that issued an order on or before May 30, 2008, against the appellant.
procedural_history.impugned_order: Final judgment and order of the High Court refusing to interfere with the order dated May 30, 2008.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court considered a revision petition against the order dated May 30, 2008, but refused to interfere with it, upholding the original order.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant, aggrieved by the High Court's decision, appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court granted leave to appeal on August 16, 2011, stayed the High Court's judgment on October 26, 2010, and ultimately allowed the appeal.

directions: The judgment and order of conviction/acquittal dated 22nd/24th February 2007 in paragraphs 49 and 50 stand quashed and set aside.
The judgment and order dated 14th October 2010 passed by the High Court in Criminal Revision No. 2194 of 2008 is quashed and set aside.
All subsequent proceedings including the order dictated and typed on 30th May 2008 by the learned Special Judge shall stand quashed and set aside.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence imposed by the Special Judge, and the subsequent order of the High Court, are liable to be set aside.

facts: A Special Judge made adverse findings against the appellant, a police officer, in a judgment dated 22nd/24th February 2007, effectively finding her guilty of an offense under Section 58 of the NDPS Act.
This finding was made without issuing any prior notice to the appellant or giving her an opportunity to be heard.
Subsequently, the Special Judge issued a notice to the appellant and conducted rushed proceedings, hearing the matter on 7 dates within a 10-day period.
The Special Judge then dictated and typed an order on 30th May 2008 and kept it in a sealed cover.
The High Court had previously dismissed the appellant's challenge to the proceedings.
law: Under Section 36-A(5) of the NDPS Act, offenses punishable with imprisonment of not more than three years, such as those under Section 58, may be tried summarily.
According to Section 260 of the Cr.P.C., the power to conduct a summary trial is vested in a Magistrate, not a Special Judge.
The principles of natural justice require that a person must be given notice and a fair opportunity to be heard before any adverse findings are made against them.
application: The Supreme Court found that the Special Judge lacked the legal jurisdiction to conduct proceedings for an offense under Section 58 of the NDPS Act, as such proceedings could only be conducted by a Magistrate through a summary trial.

The Court held that there was a "gross violation of principles of natural justice." The Special Judge acted in a "predetermined manner" by making adverse findings against the appellant before she was even notified or heard.
The rushed nature of the subsequent hearings further demonstrated a disregard for fair procedure and a "total non-application of mind."
Because the entire process was fundamentally flawed both in terms of jurisdiction and adherence to natural justice, the resulting orders were deemed unsustainable in law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the proceedings were legally invalid due to the Special Judge's lack of jurisdiction and the gross violation of the principles of natural justice. Therefore, the Court accepted the appeal and set aside the conviction and sentence imposed by the Special Judge, as well as the subsequent order of the High Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction and sentence imposed by the Special Judge, and the subsequent order of the High Court, are liable to be set aside.
appellant_arguments: The allegations against the appellant were raised for the first time during the arguments on behalf of three other accused persons who were subsequently acquitted.
The adverse findings against the appellant were recorded ex-parte, without giving her an opportunity to be heard.
respondent_arguments: The State supported the position taken by the appellant.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A judge, having dictated the operative part of a judgment of acquittal in open court, becomes functus officio and cannot subsequently recall the order and proceed with the trial.
obiter: Justice should not only be done, but also be seen to be done.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The judgment and order passed by the learned Special Judge, as well as a subsequent order dictated by him and kept in a sealed cover, are unsustainable in law for more than one reason, including a gross violation of the principles of natural justice.
legal_tests_applied: The principle that justice should not only be done but should be seen to be done.
The rule against bias, or nemo debet esse judex in propria causa (no man shall be a judge in his own cause).
policy_considerations: It is the recognition of the importance of the requirement that justice is seen to be done that justifies the giving of a remedy to a litigant even when it may be claimed that a decision alleged to be vitiated by a breach of natural justice would still have been reached had a fair hearing been given.
